facts.fact: Carl H. Eigenmann described the species as Leporinus granti in 1912.
The holotype (FMNH 53383) came from Maripicru Creek in Guyana.
The Catalog of Fishes now treats the species as valid in the genus Hypomasticus, as Hypomasticus granti, following Sidlauskas et al. (2025) and Ito et al. (2026).
The genus name Leporinus comes from the Latin lepus, leporis, meaning rabbit.
The species name honours William Grant, who guided Eigenmann on his 1908 trip to British Guiana.
The IUCN Red List assesses it as Least Concern (assessment of 2020).
A London museum specimen (BMNH 1911.10.31.465) once listed under this name is not this species.
It is one of the smaller Leporinus species in the hobby, but it still grows large and robust.
The fish traded as Leporinus sp. 'Strawberry' is closely related to, or the same as, Leporinus granti.
The video gives its native range as the Mana River in western French Guiana, on the northeast coast of South America.
FishBase lists its distribution as the Mana River basin in South America.
The Catalog of Fishes gives a range from the Orinoco River basin to French Guiana and Brazil, with records from Guyana, Suriname and Colombia, and Ecuador marked as uncertain.
Aquarium Glaser describes L. granti as known so far only from the Guianas.
Adults gather in large numbers at creek mouths over sandy or muddy bottoms, in fast or slow current.
Juveniles live in calm, shallow water, in counter-current zones or among plants.
Adults are believed to gather in large groups in creeks with sandy or muddy bottoms.
It is a rare species in the freshwater aquarium hobby.
FishBase lists it as a commercial aquarium species and says it is considered turbulent in captivity.
It is a strong jumper, so the tank needs a tightly secured lid.
Like other Leporinus, it is often wrongly stereotyped as a ferocious predator.
Because it grows large and robust, it needs a suitably sized aquarium with plenty of hiding places.
The video's keepers house it in a 450-litre aquarium.
Several pieces of bogwood and smooth rocks give it the hiding spots it needs to feel secure.
FishBase gives a temperature range of 22 to 29 °C.
FishBase gives a pH range of 5.5 to 7.5.
FishBase gives water hardness up to 20 dH.
Its diet is mainly herbivorous, and it often grazes algae in a head-down position.
When algae are scarce, it will eat plant leaves.
The video's keepers have kept it with live Cryptocoryne and Anubias plants.
It is omnivorous and not fussy, readily taking quality flakes and granules.
It also accepts live and frozen foods such as mosquito larvae, bloodworms, brine shrimp and chopped earthworms.
FishBase describes it as omnivorous and able to digest chitin, pectin, hemicellulose and mucopolysaccharides.
It is somewhat active but also shy and retiring.
Adults can be territorial towards each other, but they seem to do well kept with their own species.
Rivals spar gently by swimming side by side and rubbing against each other, rather than fighting.
Suggested tankmates are larger South American cichlids, medium to large barbs, headstanders, catfish, plecos and other Leporinus.
Small fish and fish with long, delicate fins are best avoided.
The video's keepers found that guppies living with their Leporinus were rarely disturbed and even bred, though they say this may not be typical.
The sexes are hard to tell apart.
Females tend to be slightly larger, a little less colourful and fuller-bodied than males.
FishBase gives a larger maximum length for females (25 cm TL) than for males (20 cm TL).
In the wild, it breeds from December to June.
In the wild, distinct pairs breed in densely weedy areas.
Little is known about its breeding. In the wild, it is thought to be a seasonal spawner that scatters eggs among weeds, with no parental care.
In aquaria, L. granti (or a very close relative) is said to be the only Leporinus bred successfully so far. It scatters its eggs and gives no brood care.
